board_events.text: Column I: (P) Xanthium. (Q) Spinach. (R) Sunflower. Column II: (i) Long-day plant. (ii) Day-neutral plant. (iii) Short-day plant.
P - Xanthium, the cocklebur, is the classic short-day (long-night) plant of the textbooks. So P matches (iii).
Q - Spinach flowers on long days. So Q matches (i).
R - Sunflower flowers regardless of day length. So R matches (ii).
Answer: P-iii, Q-i, R-ii.
Notice that Column II is deliberately NOT in the order you learned the categories. Never match by position - match by recall, then check that every option has been used exactly once.

segments.text: Back to the cold clock, and now with the mechanism rather than the story. Three questions: where is the cold felt, what does it actually do, and why would a plant want such a demanding arrangement?
Look at the diagram. A seedling, a cold spell, a competent apex, and flowering later - with one red arrow curving back underneath. That red arrow is devernalisation, and we will come to it.

Where is the cold perceived? Chiefly at the shoot apical meristem and in actively dividing cells. That should feel right - it is the apex that eventually has to make the decision to flower, so it is the apex that needs to remember the winter. And one extra fact that gets asked: in cereals, the embryo of the germinating seed can be vernalised directly. You do not even need a plant yet.

Now what the cold actually does, and this is the sentence to get exactly right. A sufficient spell of low temperature makes the apex competent to respond later to flowering signals. Read it again, slowly. Cold does not produce a flower. It produces the ability to respond to a flowering signal. That is a much weaker claim, and it is the true one - which is why the limiting condition from earlier said vernalisation only promotes or enables flowering. Cold is permission. The flowering signal is still the instruction.

Now the adaptive logic, which is the reasoning half of any board answer. It is timing insurance. Think it through: an autumn-sown winter cereal that flowered immediately would be trying to set seed in mid-winter, and would be destroyed. So by demanding a cold period first, it postpones flowering until the favourable spring or summer. And notice it does not waste the winter - it uses it to grow vegetatively. The plant is building itself while it waits for permission.

Then devernalisation - the reversal, or cancellation, of the vernalisation effect by exposing the plant to a higher temperature soon after the cold treatment. Follow the red arrow on the diagram: cold, competence, and then heat, and the competence is gone.

Now think about what devernalisation tells us, because this is more interesting than a definition. It proves the effect is not permanently locked in. A hot spell straight after the cold can undo it. So whatever the cold did to that apex, it was a state that could still be lost - not a switch welded shut. That fits the insurance logic rather nicely, in fact: a plant that had a brief cold snap followed by warmth has not actually been through winter, and it is better off not being fooled.

<whisper>And the examples, which are pure recall marks. Winter varieties of wheat, rye and barley - sown in autumn, vegetative through winter, flowering in summer. And biennials, such as sugar beet, cabbage and carrot. If a question mentions winter varieties or biennials, vernalisation is the answer before you have finished reading.

One short section to close the concepts, and it is the one C B S E asks for almost as a ritual. Significance. This is a point list, so learn it as a point list - but understand the shape of it first, because that is what makes it stick.
Look at the two panels. Photoperiodism on the left, the light clock. Vernalisation on the right, the cold clock. And read the strip along the bottom, because it is the sentence that unites them.

Photoperiodism first. It lets breeders make plants flower out of season, or year-round - which is why you can buy chrysanthemums in months when no field would give them. It lets crops be matched to the day-length regime of a region - so a variety is chosen to suit the latitude it will grow at. And it aids hybridisation. Think about why that last one works: to cross two parents you need them flowering at the same time, and if their natural schedules differ, controlling the photoperiod brings them into step.

Vernalisation next. It allows earlier cropping. It extends cultivation to regions where a crop would not normally flower - because if you can supply the cold artificially, you are no longer limited to places that have the right winter. It can raise yield. And it is associated with improved cold and frost resistance, and with disease resistance.

Now the framing that makes both lists memorable rather than arbitrary. Notice that both are answers to the same question: how do we take control of when a plant flowers? Photoperiodism does it by manipulating the light regime. Vernalisation does it by manipulating temperature. Two levers, one goal.

And that is exactly why these two topics are taught together, and why the board asks for them together - define photoperiodism and vernalisation, and state their significance. It looks like two questions bolted into one. It is really one question about seasonal control, asked from two directions.

<curious>So carry the mnemonic out with you, because it is small and it does a lot of work. Photoperiod equals the light clock. Vernalisation equals the cold clock. Two clocks, and the plant consults both before it commits to the most irreversible decision of its life.

A C B S E board question that the chapter says is asked almost as a ritual. Define photoperiodism and vernalisation, and give one significance of each. It is a two-to-three mark question, and it should be the easiest marks on your paper - provided you say the right two words.
Look at the diagram, because it is laid out exactly the way your answer should be. Two panels, one per phenomenon, and each with its payoffs listed. Light clock, cold clock. Answer in that shape.

Photoperiodism, definition first. It is the response of plants to the relative lengths of day and night, especially in controlling the induction of flowering. Notice relative lengths - not the length of the day, but the relation between day and night. And notice the last clause, which pins it to flowering rather than to growth generally.

Then its significance, and one concrete example is enough. It allows growers and breeders to manipulate flowering time - for instance, to produce flowers off-season. That is a real, sayable thing. Do not write that it is important for the plant's survival and stop there; the question is asking what it is good for, and vagueness scores nothing.

Vernalisation, definition. It is the promotion or induction of flowering by exposing a plant to a period of low temperature. Notice promotion or induction - the careful wording we discussed. Not causing flowering. Promoting it.
And its significance: it enables crops such as winter wheat to be grown and to flower in the correct season, and can extend a crop to new regions. Again, concrete. A named crop and a real outcome.

<whisper>Now the marking-scheme point, and this is the whole reason people drop marks on a question they know. For full marks, always link photoperiodism to day length and vernalisation to low temperature, explicitly. The examiner is scanning for those two anchor words. Write a beautiful paragraph about seasons and flowering that never says day length, and you will not get the mark - because you never proved you knew which phenomenon you were describing.

So here is the structure that scores. Definition, then the anchor word, then one concrete significance. Do that twice. Four short lines, full marks, ninety seconds - and then move on to a question that actually needs your thinking.

A C U E T match-the-column, and it is three plants against three categories. The whole thing is recall - but the paper has arranged it to punish anyone who answers by pattern rather than by knowledge.

Look at the diagram. Three plants on the left, three categories on the right, and the curved lines crossing over each other. Notice that not one of them matches straight across. That is not an accident.
Read Column one: P is Xanthium. Q is spinach. R is sunflower. And Column two: i is long-day plant, ii is day-neutral plant, iii is short-day plant.

P, Xanthium - the cocklebur. This is the classic short-day, long-night plant of the textbooks; it is the organism the whole night-break story was worked out on. Short-day plant is option three. So P matches iii.
Q, spinach. Spinach flowers on long days - it was on our long-day plant list, alongside radish, lettuce and wheat. Long-day plant is option one. So Q matches i.
R, sunflower. Sunflower flowers regardless of day length - it was on the day-neutral list with tomato, cucumber, cotton and maize. Day-neutral is option two. So R matches ii.
So the answer: P three, Q one, R two. Written out - P-iii, Q-i, R-ii.

<whisper>And now the thing worth taking away, because it generalises far beyond this question. Notice Column two is deliberately not in the order you learned the categories. You learned short-day, long-day, day-neutral. The paper lists long-day, day-neutral, short-day. If you match by position - first with first - you get every single one wrong. So never match by position. Match by recall, and then check that every option has been used exactly once. That final check catches almost every slip in this format.
वापस cold clock पर, और अब कहानी नहीं, mechanism के साथ। तीन सवाल: ठंड महसूस कहाँ होती है, वो असल में करती क्या है, और कोई plant ऐसा माँग भरा इंतज़ाम चाहेगा ही क्यों?
Diagram देखिए। एक seedling, एक cold spell, एक competent apex, और बाद में flowering - और नीचे एक red arrow मुड़ता हुआ। वही red arrow devernalisation है, उस पर आएँगे।

ठंड perceive कहाँ होती है? मुख्यतः shoot apical meristem पर और actively dividing cells में। ये सही लगना चाहिए - आख़िर फूलने का फ़ैसला apex को ही करना है, तो सर्दी याद भी apex को ही रखनी है। और एक extra fact जो पूछा जाता है: cereals में, germinating seed का embryo सीधे vernalise हो सकता है। अभी plant की ज़रूरत भी नहीं।

अब ठंड असल में करती क्या है, और यही वो वाक्य है जिसे बिलकुल सही पकड़ना है। Low temperature का पर्याप्त दौर apex को competent बना देता है कि वो बाद में flowering signals पर respond कर सके। दोबारा पढ़िए, धीरे। ठंड फूल नहीं बनाती। वो flowering signal पर respond करने की ability बनाती है। ये कहीं कमज़ोर दावा है, और यही सही है - इसीलिए पहले वाली limiting condition ने कहा था कि vernalisation सिर्फ़ flowering को promote या enable करता है। ठंड इजाज़त है। हुक्म अब भी flowering signal ही है।

अब adaptive logic, जो किसी भी board answer का reasoning वाला आधा है। ये timing insurance है। सोच कर देखिए: autumn में बोया winter cereal अगर फ़ौरन फूल जाता तो भरी सर्दी में seed बनाने की कोशिश करता, और तबाह हो जाता। तो पहले cold period माँग कर वो flowering को अनुकूल spring या summer तक टाल देता है। और notice कीजिए वो सर्दी बर्बाद नहीं करता - उसे vegetative growth में लगाता है। Plant इजाज़त का इंतज़ार करते हुए ख़ुद को बना रहा है।

फिर devernalisation - vernalisation के असर का उलट जाना या रद्द हो जाना, cold treatment के तुरंत बाद plant को ऊँचे temperature में रखने से। Diagram पर red arrow follow कीजिए: ठंड, competence, और फिर गर्मी, और competence ग़ायब।

अब सोचिए devernalisation हमें बताता क्या है, क्योंकि ये definition से ज़्यादा दिलचस्प है। ये साबित करता है कि असर स्थायी रूप से lock नहीं होता। ठंड के तुरंत बाद गर्मी का दौर उसे मिटा सकता है। तो ठंड ने उस apex के साथ जो भी किया, वो एक ऐसी हालत थी जो खो सकती थी - कोई वेल्ड किया हुआ switch नहीं। और ये insurance वाली logic में बड़ा फिट बैठता है: जिस plant को एक छोटी ठंडक के बाद गर्मी मिली, वो असल में सर्दी से गुज़रा ही नहीं, और उसका न बहकना ही बेहतर है।

<whisper>और examples, जो शुद्ध recall marks हैं। Wheat, rye और barley की winter varieties - autumn में बोई, सर्दी भर vegetative, गर्मी में flowering. और biennials, जैसे sugar beet, cabbage और carrot. Question में winter varieties या biennials आए, तो पढ़ना ख़त्म होने से पहले जवाब vernalisation है।

Concepts बंद करने के लिए एक छोटा section, और यही वो है जो C B S E लगभग रस्म की तरह पूछता है। Significance. ये point list है, तो point list की तरह ही सीखिए - पर पहले इसकी शक्ल समझिए, क्योंकि वही इसे टिकाती है।
दोनों panels देखिए। बाएँ photoperiodism, light clock. दाएँ vernalisation, cold clock. और नीचे वाली पट्टी पढ़िए, क्योंकि वही वाक्य दोनों को जोड़ता है।

पहले photoperiodism. ये breeders को plants को बेमौसम, या साल भर, फुलाने देता है - इसीलिए आप chrysanthemum उन महीनों में ख़रीद पाते हैं जब कोई खेत उन्हें नहीं देगा। ये crops को किसी इलाक़े के day-length regime से match करने देता है - यानी variety उस latitude के हिसाब से चुनी जाती है जहाँ वो उगेगी। और ये hybridisation में मदद करता है। सोचिए आख़िरी वाला काम क्यों करता है: दो parents cross करने के लिए दोनों का एक साथ फूलना ज़रूरी है, और अगर उनके natural schedules अलग हैं, तो photoperiod control करके उन्हें एक ताल पर लाया जाता है।

अब vernalisation. ये जल्दी cropping देता है। ये खेती को उन इलाक़ों तक बढ़ाता है जहाँ crop आम तौर पर फूलता ही नहीं - क्योंकि अगर ठंड artificially दी जा सके, तो आप उन्हीं जगहों तक सीमित नहीं रहे जहाँ सही सर्दी पड़ती है। ये yield बढ़ा सकता है। और ये बेहतर cold तथा frost resistance से, और disease resistance से जुड़ा है।

अब वो framing जो दोनों lists को मनमाना नहीं, यादगार बनाती है। Notice कीजिए दोनों उसी एक सवाल के जवाब हैं: plant कब फूलेगा, इस पर हम क़ाबू कैसे पाएँ? Photoperiodism ये light regime बदल कर करता है। Vernalisation temperature बदल कर। दो lever, एक मक़सद।

और ठीक इसीलिए ये दोनों topics साथ पढ़ाए जाते हैं, और board इन्हें साथ पूछता है - photoperiodism और vernalisation define कीजिए, और उनकी significance बताइए। ये दो सवाल एक में जुड़े हुए लगते हैं। असल में ये seasonal control का एक ही सवाल है, दो दिशाओं से पूछा हुआ।

<curious>तो mnemonic साथ ले जाइए, क्योंकि वो छोटा है और बहुत काम करता है। Photoperiod यानी light clock. Vernalisation यानी cold clock. दो घड़ियाँ, और plant अपनी ज़िंदगी का सबसे irreversible फ़ैसला लेने से पहले दोनों देखता है।

एक C B S E board question जिसे chapter कहता है कि लगभग रस्म की तरह पूछा जाता है। Photoperiodism और vernalisation define कीजिए, और हर एक की एक significance बताइए। ये दो-से-तीन marks का सवाल है, और आपके paper के सबसे आसान marks होने चाहिए - बशर्ते आप वो दो सही शब्द बोल दें।
Diagram देखिए, क्योंकि वो ठीक उसी शक्ल में सजा है जिसमें आपका answer होना चाहिए। दो panels, हर phenomenon के लिए एक, और हर एक के payoffs साथ। Light clock, cold clock. Answer इसी shape में दीजिए।

Photoperiodism, पहले definition. ये plants का day और night की relative lengths पर response है, ख़ास तौर पर flowering के induction को control करने में। Relative lengths notice कीजिए - day की लंबाई नहीं, बल्कि day और night का रिश्ता। और आख़िरी clause notice कीजिए, जो इसे general growth से नहीं, flowering से बाँधता है।

फिर उसकी significance, और एक ठोस उदाहरण काफ़ी है। ये growers और breeders को flowering time manipulate करने देता है - मसलन, बेमौसम फूल पैदा करना। ये असली, बोलने लायक चीज़ है। ये मत लिखिए कि plant के survival के लिए ज़रूरी है और रुक जाइए; सवाल पूछ रहा है ये किस काम का है, और गोलमोल जवाब शून्य है।

Vernalisation, definition. ये plant को low temperature के दौर में रख कर flowering का promotion या induction है। Promotion या induction notice कीजिए - वही सावधान शब्द जिन पर हमने बात की। Flowering कराना नहीं। उसे promote करना।
और उसकी significance: ये winter wheat जैसी crops को उगाने और सही मौसम में फूलने देता है, और crop को नए इलाक़ों तक बढ़ा सकता है। फिर से, ठोस। एक नामज़द crop और एक असली outcome.

<whisper>अब marking-scheme वाली बात, और यही पूरी वजह है कि लोग जाने-पहचाने सवाल में marks गँवाते हैं। पूरे marks के लिए photoperiodism को day length से और vernalisation को low temperature से हमेशा साफ़-साफ़ जोड़िए। Examiner उन्हीं दो anchor शब्दों को खोज रहा है। Seasons और flowering पर सुंदर paragraph लिख दीजिए जिसमें day length कहीं न हो, तो mark नहीं मिलेगा - क्योंकि आपने साबित ही नहीं किया कि आपको पता था आप किस phenomenon की बात कर रहे थे।
तो ये रही scoring वाली structure. Definition, फिर anchor शब्द, फिर एक ठोस significance. ये दो बार कीजिए। चार छोटी lines, पूरे marks, नब्बे seconds - और फिर उस सवाल पर बढ़िए जिसे सचमुच आपकी सोच चाहिए।
एक C U E T match-the-column, और ये तीन plants बनाम तीन categories है। पूरा का पूरा recall है - पर paper ने इसे ऐसे सजाया है कि जो ज्ञान की जगह pattern से जवाब दे, उसे सज़ा मिले।
Diagram देखिए। बाएँ तीन plants, दाएँ तीन categories, और curved lines एक दूसरे को काटती हुईं। Notice कीजिए एक भी सीधे सामने match नहीं करता। ये संयोग नहीं है।
Column one पढ़िए: P है Xanthium. Q है spinach. R है sunflower. और Column two: i है long-day plant, ii है day-neutral plant, iii है short-day plant.

P, Xanthium - यानी cocklebur. ये textbooks का classic short-day, long-night plant है; यही वो जीव है जिस पर पूरी night-break कहानी निकाली गई थी। Short-day plant option three है। तो P match करता है iii से।
Q, spinach. Spinach लंबे दिनों में फूलता है - ये हमारी long-day plant list में था, radish, lettuce और wheat के साथ। Long-day plant option one है। तो Q match करता है i से।
R, sunflower. Sunflower day length की परवाह किए बिना फूलता है - ये day-neutral list में था, tomato, cucumber, cotton और maize के साथ। Day-neutral option two है। तो R match करता है ii से।
तो answer: P three, Q one, R two. लिख कर - P-iii, Q-i, R-ii.

<whisper>और अब ले जाने लायक बात, क्योंकि ये इस सवाल से कहीं आगे तक लागू होती है। Notice कीजिए Column two जानबूझ कर उस order में नहीं है जिसमें आपने categories सीखी थीं। आपने सीखा short-day, long-day, day-neutral. Paper ने रखा long-day, day-neutral, short-day. अगर आपने position से match किया - पहले को पहले से - तो हर एक ग़लत। तो कभी position से match मत कीजिए। Recall से match कीजिए, और फिर check कीजिए कि हर option ठीक एक बार इस्तेमाल हुआ है। वही आख़िरी check इस format की लगभग हर चूक पकड़ लेता है।

board_events.text: N E E T: the single most-tested idea in the subtopic

A short-day plant is kept under a long continuous dark period and flowers normally. In a second trial, the long dark period is interrupted by a one-minute flash of light at its midpoint. Predict the result and justify.

board_events.text: Step 1 - translate the label. A short-day plant is in truth a LONG-NIGHT plant. What it requires is an UNINTERRUPTED dark period longer than its critical value.
Step 2 - read what the flash does. The midnight flash - a NIGHT BREAK - resets its measurement of continuous darkness. The effective dark period is now two short stretches, not one long one.
Step 3 - conclude. Therefore the plant FAILS to flower, even though the total hours of darkness barely changed.
Answer: No flowering - the night break destroys the required continuous dark period.
The justification is the mark. 'No flowering' alone is a guess; 'no flowering because continuity, not total, is what is measured' is an answer.
N E E T high-difficulty: assertion and reason
ASSERTION (A): A plant whose every leaf has been removed will not flower even under a fully inductive photoperiod.
REASON (R): The shoot apical meristem is the site that perceives the photoperiodic stimulus.

board_events.text: Is A true? YES. Without leaves there is no organ to perceive the photoperiod, so no florigen is produced, and flowering cannot be triggered.
Is R true? NO. The site of perception is the LEAF, not the shoot apex. The apex is where flowers eventually FORM - but it does not perceive the light signal.
So A is true and R is false.
Answer: Option (3) - A true, R false.
Trap: students who half-remember 'apex means flowers' wrongly mark R true and pick option (1). The assertion being true makes the false reason feel true by association.
Where students actually lose these marks

PITFALL 1 - 'short-day' does NOT mean few hours of light. The label is relative to each plant's OWN critical day length, and the dark period is what actually counts. Always translate SDP to 'long-night' and LDP to 'short-night' in your head BEFORE answering.
PITFALL 2 - the wrong site of perception. Light is perceived by LEAVES; flowers FORM at the shoot apex. Examiners deliberately swap these.
PITFALL 3 - confusing the two phenomena. Photoperiodism = response to DAY LENGTH. Vernalisation = response to LOW TEMPERATURE. If a question mentions cold or winter, it is vernalisation, full stop.
PITFALL 4 - forgetting day-neutral plants exist. When a question says 'flowers in all photoperiods', that is a DNP - not a trick.

PRO-TIP: for any 'will it flower?' question, ignore the light hours first. Ask only - was the CONTINUOUS DARK period long enough (for an SDP) or short enough (for an LDP)? Then check for a NIGHT BREAK: a single flash flips the answer.
That two-step check - continuous dark, then night break - resolves almost every photoperiod problem in seconds.
Mnemonic: 'SDP = Sleeps in Darkness Plenty' (it needs long nights). And: photoperiod = light clock, vernalisation = cold clock.
Plant Growth and Development - the night-before card
GROWTH = permanent, irreversible increase in size. Plant growth is OPEN, INDETERMINATE, INTRINSIC and LOCALISED (at meristems). Phases: meristematic, elongation, maturation.

board_events.emphasis: ARITHMETIC growth - a STRAIGHT LINE. Only one daughter cell continues to divide.
GEOMETRIC growth - SIGMOID in nature. Both daughters divide. Phases: lag, log, diminishing, stationary.
AGR is total growth per unit time; RGR is growth per unit existing biomass. Efficiency index = r.

board_events.text: DIFFERENTIATION (commit to a function) to DEDIFFERENTIATION (regain division - cambia) to REDIFFERENTIATION (lose division again - secondary xylem, cork). DEVELOPMENT = growth + differentiation. PLASTICITY gives heterophylly (cotton, coriander, larkspur). Order mnemonic: 'Di-El-Di-Ma-Se'. Direction: DE = Division Enabled; RE = Retired.

AUXINS (IAA/IBA natural; NAA, 2,4-D synthetic; POLAR transport): cell elongation, apical dominance, rooting, parthenocarpy, 2,4-D weedicide. GIBBERELLINS (GA3; terpene; acidic): bolting, dwarf to tall, breaks dormancy, alpha-amylase in cereals. CYTOKININS (zeatin natural, kinetin synthetic; purine; basic): cell division, delays senescence (Richmond-Lang), overcomes apical dominance. Coconut milk = cytokinin.

ETHYLENE ($C_2H_4$; gas; from methionine; ethephon): ripening, senescence, abscission, female flowers, pineapple flowering. ABA (carotenoid derivative; stress hormone; acidic): dormancy + stomatal closure; antagonist of GA. RATIO RULE: high auxin:cytokinin gives ROOTS; high cytokinin:auxin gives SHOOTS. BIOASSAYS: auxin - Avena curvature; GA - dwarf pea/corn; cytokinin - cell-division test. Mnemonics: 'A-G-C go'; 'ABA and Ethylene halt'.

PHOTOPERIODISM = flowering response to relative day/night length; perceived by LEAVES (even one), signalled by FLORIGEN to the shoot apex; pigment = PHYTOCHROME. SDP = long-night plants (flower BELOW critical day length): chrysanthemum, Xanthium, rice, soybean, Maryland Mammoth tobacco. LDP = short-night plants (flower ABOVE it): spinach, radish, lettuce, wheat, sugar beet, Hyoscyamus. DNP: any photoperiod - tomato, cucumber, sunflower, cotton, maize.

NIGHT BREAK: a flash in mid-darkness stops flowering in SDP and can induce it in LDP - proving the DARK period is decisive. VERNALISATION = low-temperature promotion of flowering (winter wheat/rye/barley; biennials such as sugar beet, cabbage); reversible by heat = DEVERNALISATION. Mnemonics: 'SDP = Sleeps in Darkness Plenty'; photoperiod = light clock, vernalisation = cold clock.

segments.text: An N E E T question, and the chapter tells you plainly that this is the single most-tested idea in the subtopic. So let us do it properly, and let us do it in a way you could reproduce under pressure.

The question. A short-day plant is kept under a long continuous dark period, and it flowers normally. In a second trial, the long dark period is interrupted by a one-minute flash of light at its midpoint. Predict the result and justify.
Look at the bars - bar one and bar three of the top set. This is exactly the experiment in the question, drawn out. Baseline, and night break. Now work in three steps.

Step one: translate the label, and do this before anything else. A short-day plant is in truth a long-night plant. So restate what it actually requires: an uninterrupted dark period longer than its critical value. Notice that once you have written that sentence, the question is nearly solved - because now you know exactly what to check.

Step two: read what the flash does to that requirement. The midnight flash - a night break - resets the plant's measurement of continuous darkness. So the effective dark period is now two short stretches, not one long one. Neither stretch is long enough. The requirement fails.

Step three: conclude. Therefore the plant fails to flower - even though the total hours of darkness barely changed. And that clause matters, because it is where the marks are. A one-minute flash removes one minute of darkness. Almost nothing. And yet the answer flips completely.
So: no flowering. The night break destroys the required continuous dark period.

<whisper>And now the part that separates a two-mark answer from a full one. The justification is the mark. Writing no flowering alone is a guess - and half the hall guesses that, because it feels like the trick answer. Writing no flowering because continuity, not total, is what the plant measures - that is an answer. It shows you know why the flash matters. Never give the verdict without the reason on a question like this.
The last worked example of the chapter, and it is an assertion-reason - so we run the same three-question method one final time. Is A true? Is R true? Does R explain A?
Assertion A: a plant whose every leaf has been removed will not flower, even under a fully inductive photoperiod. Hold it.

Reason R: the shoot apical meristem is the site that perceives the photoperiodic stimulus. Now, before you go any further - notice that R is a factual claim about anatomy, and it is completely checkable. That is your way in.

Look at the diagram while we work. Left panel, the assertion, marked true. Right panel, the reason, marked false in red. And underneath, the two organs separated out: what perceives, and what forms flowers.

Question one: is A true? Yes. And justify it with the chain: without leaves there is no organ to perceive the photoperiod, so no florigen is produced, and flowering cannot be triggered. The plant is blind, not sick. So the assertion stands - and notice how easy that was, which is exactly what makes this question dangerous.

Question two: is R true? No. And this is the whole question. The site of perception is the leaf, not the shoot apex. R has named the wrong organ. The apex is where flowers eventually form - that part is true - but it does not perceive the light signal. R has taken a true fact about the apex and attached it to the wrong job.
So A is true and R is false. And notice we never even reached the third question - if R is false, there is nothing for it to explain. The method terminates early.
The answer is option three: A true, R false.

<whisper>Now the trap, and it is beautifully built. Students who half-remember apex means flowers will mark R true and pick option one. And think about why they fall for it: the assertion is true, and it feels connected to the reason, so the reason feels true by association. That is the whole mechanism of this trap. A true assertion lends its credibility to a false reason. So evaluate R entirely on its own, before you ever look at how well it fits A.
Let us close the subtopic with the four places students actually lose these marks. Same discipline as the previous parts - not more content, just the failure modes.

Pitfall one, and it is the big one: short-day does not mean few hours of light. The label is relative to each plant's own critical day length, and the dark period is what actually counts. So build a habit - always translate S D P to long-night, and L D P to short-night, in your head, before you answer anything. Do the translation first and half the traps in this subtopic simply stop working.

Pitfall two: the wrong site of perception. Light is perceived by leaves. Flowers form at the shoot apex. Two organs, two jobs, and examiners deliberately swap them - we just watched an entire assertion-reason question built on exactly that swap. If a statement puts perception at the apex, it is false, however confident it sounds.

Pitfall three: confusing the two phenomena. Photoperiodism is the response to day length. Vernalisation is the response to low temperature. And here is a rule you can apply without thinking: if a question mentions cold, or winter, it is vernalisation. Full stop. The two get taught together, which is exactly why they get muddled together.

Pitfall four, and it is the mistake of an over-prepared student: forgetting that day-neutral plants exist. When a question says a plant flowers in all photoperiods, that is a day-neutral plant. It is not a trick, it is not a special case, it is the third category. Some students stare at it looking for the catch and talk themselves out of the right answer.

<excited>Now the pro-tip, and this one is worth the whole section. For any will-it-flower question, ignore the light hours first. Completely. Ask only one thing: was the continuous dark period long enough - for an S D P - or short enough - for an L D P? Then check for a night break, because a single flash flips the answer.

That is a two-step check. Continuous dark, then night break. And it resolves almost every photoperiod problem in seconds, because it asks the plant's question rather than the paper's question. The paper will hand you light hours to distract you. The plant never looked at them.

And the mnemonics to carry out of the chapter. S D P equals Sleeps in Darkness Plenty - it needs long nights. And the pair we have used throughout: photoperiod is the light clock, vernalisation is the cold clock. Two lines, and the backbone of this subtopic is portable.

This is the last section of the chapter, so let us put the whole thing on one card. Nothing new here - this is the night-before page, and if a line on it surprises you, that is the line to go back to.

Growth: a permanent, irreversible increase in size. And the four adjectives that make plant growth distinctive - it is open, indeterminate, intrinsic and localised, localised meaning it happens at meristems. Phases: meristematic, elongation, maturation.
The first kinetic. L sub t equals L nought plus r t - arithmetic growth, and it plots as a straight line. It happens when only one daughter cell continues to divide while the other matures.

The second. W sub one equals W nought e to the r t - geometric growth, which gives the sigmoid curve in nature because resources eventually run short. Both daughters divide here. And the four phases of that curve: lag, log, diminishing, stationary.

The two rates. A G R is the difference in weight over the time interval - total growth per unit time. R G R divides that same growth by the starting biomass and multiplies by one hundred - growth per unit of existing material. And the efficiency index is r. If you remember nothing else about these two: A G R asks how much, R G R asks how much for its size.

The differentiation trio, and the direction matters more than the words. Differentiation - a cell commits to a function. Dedifferentiation - a mature cell regains the ability to divide, giving you the cambia. Redifferentiation - it loses that ability again, giving secondary xylem and cork. Development equals growth plus differentiation. Plasticity gives heterophylly, in cotton, coriander and larkspur. Order mnemonic: Di-El-Di-Ma-Se. Direction mnemonic: D E means Division Enabled, R E means Retired.

The three promoters. Auxins - I A A and I B A natural, N A A and two four D synthetic, polar transport - do cell elongation, apical dominance, rooting, parthenocarpy, and two four D is the weedicide. Gibberellins - G A three, terpene, acidic - do bolting, dwarf to tall, break dormancy, and alpha-amylase in cereals. Cytokinins - zeatin natural, kinetin synthetic, purine, basic - do cell division, delay senescence via the Richmond-Lang effect, and overcome apical dominance. And coconut milk means cytokinin.

The two inhibitors, plus the switch. Ethylene - C two H four, a gas, made from methionine, supplied as ethephon - does ripening, senescence, abscission, female flowers, and pineapple flowering. A B A - carotenoid derivative, the stress hormone, acidic - does dormancy and stomatal closure, and is the antagonist of G A. The ratio rule: high auxin to cytokinin gives roots; high cytokinin to auxin gives shoots. Bioassays: auxin by Avena curvature, G A by dwarf pea or corn, cytokinin by the cell-division test. And the mnemonics: A-G-C go; A B A and Ethylene halt.

Photoperiodism: the flowering response to relative day and night length. Perceived by leaves - even one is enough - signalled by florigen to the shoot apex, and the pigment is phytochrome. S D P are long-night plants, flowering below their critical day length: chrysanthemum, Xanthium, rice, soybean, Maryland Mammoth tobacco. L D P are short-night plants, flowering above it: spinach, radish, lettuce, wheat, sugar beet, Hyoscyamus. D N P flower in any photoperiod: tomato, cucumber, sunflower, cotton, maize.

And the close. Night break: a flash in mid-darkness stops flowering in an S D P and can induce it in an L D P - which is the proof that the dark period is decisive. Vernalisation: the low-temperature promotion of flowering - winter wheat, rye and barley, and biennials such as sugar beet and cabbage - and it is reversible by heat, which is devernalisation. Two mnemonics to finish: S D P equals Sleeps in Darkness Plenty. And photoperiod is the light clock, vernalisation the cold clock. That is the chapter. Go and use it.

Step one: label का अनुवाद कीजिए, और ये सबसे पहले। Short-day plant असल में long-night plant है। तो दोबारा लिखिए कि उसे चाहिए क्या: अपने critical value से लंबा uninterrupted dark period. Notice कीजिए ये वाक्य लिख देने के बाद सवाल लगभग हल है - क्योंकि अब आपको पता है check क्या करना है।
